title: Ordinary cookies and opaque cookies with no stated role
summary: Synthetic Cookie headers with preference, consent and locale cookies, and one with a cookie of an application-specific name holding a 32-character opaque value.
rationale: Not every cookie is an authentication secret, but the standard assigns no meaning to names and says non-nonce cookie content might itself be sensitive. Preference cookies are plausibly benign and an opaque value under an unknown name could be a session identifier; the sources settle neither, so no outcome is frozen and the name-to-role mapping is a maintainer decision.

expectation.rationale: No outcome is asserted. RFC 6265 leaves cookie semantics to the application and notes that non-nonce content might be sensitive; a third-party guide lists common session cookie names but is a lead, not a rule. Candidate for the preference cookies: expected unflagged under a maintainer policy; the opaque value has no candidate outcome. Needs a maintainer decision.

sources.supports: The semantics of individual cookies in the Cookie header are not defined by this document
non-nonce cookie content, which might itself be sensitive
session ID names used by the most common web application development frameworks can be easily fingerprinted, such as PHPSESSID, JSESSIONID

notes: Project-authored by the Redact Secret project, which maintains this repository; not independent evidence. Draft; not yet reviewed. Authored from the cited standards read on 2026-10-03, before any scanner was consulted. All values are synthetic and were not tested against any service. Header coalescing, parser and action policy, decoded-token mapping and product masking stay with the downstream repositories.
